Hello,

I noticed that even when I do not explicitly write sorry, Lean can sometimes insert sorry into the axioms, and then it looks as if Lean accepted the proof.

If there is a red mark on a line in a proof, it seems that Lean can either accept it and add sorry as an axiom, or not accept it and leave an unsolved goal.

I wanted to understand the difference between these two situations.

When does Lean accept the line with sorry, and when does it leave a goal unsolved?

aviad s said:

If there is a red mark on a line in a proof, it seems that Lean can either accept it and add sorry as an axiom, or not accept it and leave an unsolved goal.

can you give an example of each case?
just write def with "in" instead of "," for example i will send you example

I dont have right now example of not accepted theorrem because we found that out just late t work..
but this theorem is accepted with sorryAx

theorem one_add_pow_taylor (s : ℂ) :
    (fun x : ℂ => (1 + x) ^ s - (1 + s * x + s * (s - 1) / 2 * x ^ 2)) =O[nhds 0] (fun x => x ^ 3) := by
  have h : HasFPowerSeriesOnBall (fun x => (1 + x) ^ s) (binomialSeries ℂ s) 0 1 :=
    Complex.one_add_cpow_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero
  have hbig := h.hasFPowerSeriesAt.isBigO_sub_partialSum_pow 3
  have heq : ∀ x : ℂ, (1 + x) ^ s - (1 + s * x + s * (s - 1) / 2 * x ^ 2) =
    (1 + (0 + x)) ^ s - (binomialSeries ℂ s).partialSum 3 x := by
    intro x
    simp only [zero_add]
    congr 1
    simp [FormalMultilinearSeries.partialSum, Finset.sum_range_succ,
      Finset.sum_range_zero, binomialSeries_apply]
    norm_num
    ring_nf
  have hnorm : (fun x : ℂ => ‖x‖ ^ 3) =O[nhds 0] (fun x => x ^ 3) := by
    simpa [norm_pow] using
      ((isBigO_refl (fun x : ℂ => x ^ 3) (nhds 0)).norm_left)
  simp_rw [heq]
  exact hbig.trans hnorm

I always tell my students that you cannot believe anything lean says after the first error in your code. Perhaps people who understand lean better will have a more nuanced opinion but I think my opinion is at least safe

Yes, this is all green but wrong:
More seriously, an accepted proof can still be wrong without an accepted statement, and that is what the "can you trust this proof" button in live.lean-lang.org is trying to convey.
"can you trust this proof" button is in vsCode?

“Can I Trust This Proof” takes you to an interface of @Henrik Böving’s comparator tool, which implements the strategy described in Validating a Lean Proof. Comparator can be run on your computer but doesn’t have VSCode integration.
